questions.stem: How can cells in an early embryo develop into different cell types while retaining the same genome?

options.text: Morphogen gradients cause different patterns of gene expression in cells at different positions
options.why: Different morphogen concentrations regulate which genes are expressed. The resulting proteins lead cells along different pathways of differentiation.

options.text: Mitosis distributes different sets of genes to cells in different parts of the embryo
options.why: Mitosis normally preserves the genome in each daughter cell. The cells differ because they express different genes, not because they receive different ones.

options.text: Each specialized cell removes the genes that are unnecessary for its mature function
options.why: Specialized cells usually retain the organism's genome. Genes can be inactive without being removed from the DNA.

options.text: Environmental signals alter the genetic code until each cell contains suitable proteins
options.why: Differentiation doesn't require the genetic code to be rewritten. Signals regulate the use of existing genes.

questions.stem: Which pair of properties defines a stem cell?

options.text: Self-renewal and the capacity to differentiate
options.why: A stem cell can maintain an unspecialized stem-cell population and produce specialized descendants.

options.text: Unlimited growth and absence of a plasma membrane
options.why: Stem cells have plasma membranes like other cells. Uncontrolled growth describes a feature of tumors, not a defining stem-cell property.

options.text: Rapid metabolism and the inability to undergo mitosis
options.why: Stem cells must divide for self-renewal and production of differentiating cells. A high metabolic rate isn't part of the definition.

options.text: A haploid nucleus and the ability to fuse with another cell
options.why: Those features describe gametes involved in fertilization. Stem cells are generally diploid cells in embryos or tissues.

questions.stem: What is the function of a stem cell niche in adult tissue?

options.text: It maintains stem cells and regulates their proliferation and differentiation
options.why: The niche provides the local cells and signals that preserve a stem-cell pool or activate it when new specialized cells are needed.

options.text: It converts every adult stem cell into a totipotent embryonic cell
options.why: Adult stem cells are commonly multipotent. A niche regulates their existing behavior rather than turning them all into totipotent cells.

options.text: It stores mature cells permanently so that they cannot divide or die
options.why: A niche houses and regulates stem cells, not a permanent store of mature cells. Its role includes controlled proliferation and differentiation.

options.text: It prevents chemical signals from reaching stem cells in the tissue
options.why: Signals within the niche help control stem-cell behavior. Blocking all signaling would remove that regulation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes pluripotent from multipotent stem cells?

options.text: Pluripotent cells form all three germ layers; multipotent cells form a few related types
options.why: Pluripotent cells have a broader developmental range. Multipotent cells, such as haemopoietic stem cells, are restricted to related lineages.

options.text: Pluripotent cells form a whole organism, whereas multipotent cells form all body-cell types
options.why: The ability to form a whole organism belongs to totipotent cells. Multipotent cells have the narrower range, not all body-cell types.

options.text: Pluripotent cells occur only in adults, whereas multipotent cells occur only in early embryos
options.why: This reverses the usual examples. Pluripotent cells occur in the early embryo, while adult bone marrow contains multipotent stem cells.

options.text: Pluripotent cells cannot differentiate, whereas multipotent cells can produce any specialized cell
options.why: Both types can differentiate. Pluripotent cells have the broader range, while multipotent cells produce a restricted set.

questions.stem: A cube-shaped cell has a side length of 4 µm. What is its surface area-to-volume ratio?

options.why: Its surface area is 6 × 4² = 96 µm² and its volume is 4³ = 64 µm³. The ratio 96:64 simplifies to 1.5:1.
This uses the side length as the ratio without calculating surface area and volume. Both quantities must be calculated first.
A 1 µm cube has a ratio of 6:1. The ratio falls as the cube's side length increases.
Sixteen is the area of one face, not the ratio. A cube has six faces and a volume calculated by cubing its side length.

questions.stem: Why can a decreasing surface area-to-volume ratio limit cell size?

options.text: Exchange capacity rises with membrane area, while metabolic demand rises mainly with cell volume
options.why: Volume increases faster than surface area as a cell grows. The membrane may then be unable to supply or clear the larger volume fast enough.

options.text: Large cells lose all membrane area and can no longer exchange substances with their surroundings
options.why: Large cells have more total membrane area, not none. They have less membrane area relative to each unit of volume.

options.text: Metabolic demand depends only on surface area, while exchange depends entirely on cytoplasmic volume
options.why: The relationship is reversed. Exchange occurs across membrane area, while the amount of active cell material is related to volume.

options.text: Volume increases with length squared, while surface area increases with length cubed
options.why: Surface area scales with length squared and volume with length cubed. That difference makes the ratio decrease.

questions.stem: Which adaptation increases the surface area available for selective reabsorption by a proximal convoluted tubule cell?

options.text: A brush border of microvilli
options.why: Microvilli are projections of the plasma membrane. They add membrane area for transport during selective reabsorption.

options.text: A biconcave shape without a nucleus
options.why: That describes an erythrocyte adaptation for oxygen transport and flexibility. It isn't the brush border of a kidney tubule cell.

options.text: A long axon covered by myelin
options.why: That describes a neuron specialized for rapid signaling over distance. It doesn't increase kidney reabsorption.

options.text: A tail containing a bending axoneme
options.why: That describes sperm propulsion. An axoneme moves a flagellum rather than increasing absorptive membrane area.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly matches an alveolar cell with its adaptation?

options.text: Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin, reducing the diffusion distance for respiratory gases
options.why: Type I pneumocytes form most of the thin gas-exchange surface. Their flattened shape shortens the path between alveolar air and blood.

options.text: Type II pneumocytes are extremely thin, allowing them to transport oxygen with haemoglobin
options.why: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant rather than transport oxygen with haemoglobin. Erythrocytes contain haemoglobin.

options.text: Type I pneumocytes contain lamellar bodies that release surfactant into capillaries
options.why: Lamellar bodies occur in type II pneumocytes and release surfactant into the alveolar lumen, not into capillaries.

options.text: Type II pneumocytes contain myofibrils that contract and inflate the alveoli
options.why: Myofibrils are contractile structures in muscle. Type II pneumocytes help alveoli remain open by secreting surfactant.

questions.stem: Why does alveolar tissue contain both type I and type II pneumocytes?

options.text: The tissue needs both a thin diffusion surface and cells specialized for surfactant secretion
options.why: The two jobs need different structures. Extreme thinness favors rapid diffusion, while secretion requires vesicles and more cytoplasm.

options.text: Type I cells exchange oxygen, while type II cells exchange carbon dioxide through a separate pathway
options.why: Both respiratory gases diffuse across the thin alveolar surface. Type II cells are distinguished by surfactant secretion.

options.text: Type I cells function during inhalation, while type II cells replace them during exhalation
options.why: The two cell types don't alternate with each breath. They perform different structural and secretory roles in the same tissue.

options.text: One cell type lines arteries, while the other forms the muscle that ventilates the lungs
options.why: Both are epithelial cells in alveoli. Ventilation depends on respiratory muscles, not pneumocytes becoming muscle.

questions.stem: Which comparison between cardiac muscle cells and striated skeletal muscle fibres is accurate?

options.text: Cardiac cells are short and branched, while skeletal fibres are long, unbranched and multinucleate
options.why: Cardiac cells form a branching network and usually have one nucleus. Skeletal fibres form through cell fusion and therefore contain many nuclei.

options.text: Cardiac cells lack myofibrils, while skeletal fibres contain myofibrils for contraction
options.why: Both muscle types contain contractile myofibrils. Their branching, length and number of nuclei differ.

options.text: Cardiac cells are fused into long multinucleate fibres, while skeletal fibres remain separate
options.why: This reverses the developmental pattern. Skeletal fibres form by fusion, while cardiac muscle contains connected individual cells.

options.text: Cardiac cells are long and unbranched, while skeletal fibres form a three-dimensional branching network
options.why: This reverses their shapes. Cardiac cells branch, while skeletal muscle fibres run as long unbranched units.

questions.stem: What provides the strongest evidence that a striated skeletal muscle fibre differs from a typical single cell?

options.text: It forms by fusion of precursor cells and has many nuclei
options.why: Fusion explains its unusual multinucleate condition. The fibre still acts as one unit enclosed by a continuous membrane.

options.text: It contains myofibrils that generate force during contraction
options.why: Myofibrils explain contraction but don't settle whether the fibre is a typical cell. Cardiac muscle cells contain myofibrils too.

options.text: It exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide across its outer surface
options.why: Gas exchange across a membrane is common to cells and doesn't explain the classification problem. Fusion and multiple nuclei do.

options.text: It expresses genes and synthesizes proteins in its cytoplasm
options.why: Those are ordinary cellular activities. They don't distinguish a muscle fibre from a typical single cell.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly links sperm structures to their functions?

options.text: Acrosome enzymes aid penetration, midpiece mitochondria supply ATP, and axoneme bending provides propulsion
options.why: Each region has a different job in reaching and fertilizing the egg. The tail's axoneme produces movement using energy supplied through metabolism.

options.text: Acrosome mitochondria supply ATP, the midpiece stores DNA, and the tail prevents polyspermy
options.why: The structures have been reassigned. The nucleus stores paternal DNA, midpiece mitochondria support movement, and the egg's cortical response helps prevent polyspermy.

options.text: The acrosome produces surfactant, the midpiece absorbs nutrients, and the tail carries maternal DNA
options.why: Surfactant belongs to alveoli, and maternal DNA comes from the egg. The sperm head carries paternal DNA.

options.text: The acrosome forms microvilli, the midpiece releases enzymes, and the tail completes meiosis
options.why: Microvilli are membrane projections in absorptive cells. Acrosome enzymes aid penetration, and tail movement doesn't complete meiosis.

questions.stem: Which feature of the human egg helps prevent fertilization by additional sperm after one sperm has fused?

options.text: Release of material from cortical granules
options.why: Cortical granules release their contents after sperm fusion. The resulting changes to the egg's surroundings help block polyspermy.

options.text: ATP production by midpiece mitochondria
options.why: A mitochondrial midpiece is a sperm adaptation for movement. It isn't part of the egg's block to polyspermy.

options.text: Contraction of myofibrils beneath the zona pellucida
options.why: Myofibrils are muscle structures. The egg uses a cortical-granule response rather than muscle contraction.

options.text: Secretion of surfactant from lamellar bodies
options.why: Lamellar bodies release surfactant from type II pneumocytes in alveoli. They aren't responsible for preventing polyspermy.
